newsitem.title: INDIA: Airliners collide over India, 350 feared dead.
newsitem.headline: Airliners collide over India, 350 feared dead.

text.p: Around 350 people were feared killed on Tuesday when a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet taking off from New Delhi and an incoming Kazakh airliner smashed into each other in the world's worst mid-air collision.

Wreckage and burning bodies, some recognisable as women and children, were spread over six km (four miles) of woodland near the village of Charkhi Dadri in Haryana State, some 80 km (50 miles) from New Delhi. Rescue workers battling flames recovered 275 bodies by late Tuesday evening, United News of India reported.
"There is hardly any chance of survivors," an Indian official said.
Villagers crowded around the crash site and more than 300 police cordoned off the area where the impact had ploughed up craters 10 feet deep.
A U.S. Air Force pilot flying nearby saw two fireballs plunge to earth from an altitude some 15,000 feet above northern India.

"In the distance off our right-hand side, two fireballs seemed to appear ... diverging away from each other," the pilot, who was bringing a military cargo plane into New Delhi, told reporters in Washington by telephone.
"The two fireballs proceeded to descend down and hit the ground and became fireballs on the ground," he said.
Officials said there were 312 people, including 23 crew, aboard the Saudi Arabian Airlines flight SV 763, a Boeing 747.
The plane was bound for Dhahran and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. Most of the passengers were Indians and Nepalese.
Kazakh Airlines flight KZA 1907, a Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane, carried 28 passengers and 10 crew, according to transport officials in the Central Asian state.
It was flying from Chimkent in Kazakhstan to New Delhi but had been chartered by a company in neighbouring Kyrgyzstan and most of the passengers aboard were Kyrgyz.
PTI said there were 17 foreigners on the 747.
If the toll of 350 is confirmed, the air disaster will be among the world's five worst for loss of life and the worst involving two aircraft in flight.

Ranjan Chatterjee, chairman of Airports Authority of India said: "We have not heard of any survivors so far. It seems rather difficult, unfortunately. Coming from that height of 14,000 to 15,000 feet chances of survival do not appear to be very bright."
He said air traffic control equipment had been functioning normally.
Officials of the directorate general of civil aviation said the Saudi airliner had been cleared to climb to 14,000 feet (4,270 metres) by air traffic control in New Delhi.
They said the Kazakh airliner had been cleared to descend to 15,000 feet (4,570 metres).
"Radar blips of both aircraft disappeared at 1840 hrs (1310 GMT), 40 nautical miles southwest of Delhi," one official said.
An eyewitness quoted by the PTI said: "I saw a ball of flame hurtling down and I could make out that it was an aircraft."
The Indian government has ordered an inquiry into the collision, aviation officials said.
The previous worst mid-air accident was when a British Trident and a Yugoslav DC9 collided over Zagreb in 1976 with the loss of 176 lives.
